request.title: A leaf trades water for carbon
request.topic: Write a roughly 2-minute lesson in exactly 3 scenes for a curious 12-year-old. Explain how opening stomata lets carbon dioxide enter for photosynthesis while water vapor escapes, and why closing them in dry conditions protects water but restricts carbon uptake. Show the causal tradeoff rather than list plant parts. No equations and no scripted pauses. Do not imply plants consciously decide, that stomata are one-way valves, or that closing instantly stops all water loss.

# A leaf trades water for carbon

## Beat 1 — One opening, two consequences

Content needed: One schematic broad leaf and a selected patch of its lower surface. Introduce a single open stoma as a gap between two guard cells, continuous with air spaces inside the leaf. Preserve this patch and pore for the following scenes. Do not show gas-flow answers yet.

Narration: A leaf needs carbon dioxide from the air to make sugar. But letting that gas in can let water out. How can the same tiny opening do both?

## Beat 2 — A shared passage

Content needed: Continue into the selected pore and a schematic cutaway of the moist interior. Identify stomata, then show carbon dioxide entering and being used in photosynthesis, followed by water evaporating and water vapor escaping through the same opening. Use irregular gas motion in both directions; any arrows represent overall movement, not one-way permission. Particle counts and sizes are illustrative.

Narration: These openings are called stomata. An open stoma connects outside air with spaces inside the leaf. There, cells use light energy to make sugars from carbon dioxide and water. As photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide, more can move in from the outside air.

Narration: Meanwhile, water evaporates from moist surfaces inside the leaf. When the outside air is drier, more water vapor moves out than comes back in. Gas molecules move in both directions through the opening; these arrows show the overall movement. So the pore does not separate useful carbon dioxide from escaping water. The same open passage allows both exchanges. That is why gaining carbon can cost the leaf water.

## Beat 3 — Narrowing the passage

Content needed: Keep the same pore, guard cells, moist interior, and gas identities. Make the outside air drier, showing fewer water-vapor particles outside and a greater tendency for outward loss while the pore is still open. Then show the guard cells changing shape and narrowing the pore in response to dry-condition signals. Show both exchanges becoming more restricted, and retain a small amount of water loss through the leaf surface. End on the same leaf and selected patch with the tradeoff visible, without numerical rates.

Narration: Now imagine the air becomes much drier. With less water vapor outside, water escapes more readily through an open pore. If the leaf loses water faster than its roots replace it, it can dry out.

Narration: In dry conditions, signals can make the two guard cells around a pore lose water and change shape, narrowing the opening. This is a physical response, with no thinking or planning involved.

Narration: A narrower passage slows water loss, but also limits fresh carbon dioxide entering, so photosynthesis can slow. Closing stomata does not instantly stop every water loss: some water still escapes through the leaf's outer surface. Opening gives carbon dioxide easier access at a water cost; closing helps conserve water while restricting that access.

plan.learningGoal: Explain why an open stoma supports carbon dioxide uptake while allowing water-vapor loss, and predict why narrowing it in dry conditions conserves water while restricting carbon uptake.
plan.centralQuestion: Why does the same opening that gives a leaf carbon dioxide also cost it water?
plan.keyInsight: An open pore connects the moist interior with outside air and permits gases to move both ways. Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide inside while evaporation supplies water vapor; their different inside-outside conditions produce opposite overall movements. Narrowing the shared passage restricts both exchanges.
plan.runningExample: One idealized broad leaf with a selected lower-surface stoma, first open in air drier than the leaf interior and then narrowing as conditions become much drier. Particle sizes, spacing, and counts are qualitative, with no measured rates or anatomical dimensions implied.

# A leaf trades water for carbon

## Beat 1 — An opening with two consequences

Content needed: A schematic leaf with one selected stoma on its lower surface, enlarged into a connected cutaway. Show paired guard cells around an open pore, moist internal cell surfaces, and connected internal air spaces. Establish outside air containing carbon dioxide and internal air containing abundant water vapor. Reveal net carbon dioxide entry and net water vapor exit only with the corresponding narration. Molecules move in both directions; emphasize the net flows without treating the opening as a valve.

Narration: A leaf needs carbon dioxide from the air to make sugars through photosynthesis. But its outer covering makes it difficult for gases to pass straight through. Tiny openings called stomata provide a route inside. Here is one, enlarged, with two guard cells surrounding the opening. Beyond it are air spaces beside the leaf's cells. While photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide inside, more can enter from outside. That same open route also lets water vapor escape. So the opening helps the leaf get an ingredient for making sugar, but it also creates a route for losing water.

## Beat 2 — Why water keeps leaving

Content needed: Retain the same open pore and internal air spaces. Show a small amount of water evaporating from moist cell surfaces into internal air, followed by net vapor diffusion through the pore. Show carbon dioxide being taken up at photosynthesizing cells, maintaining net entry. Compare the same pore under less dry and drier outside air, holding its opening and temperature constant. Do not use equations or numerical readouts.

Narration: Why does water keep leaving? Inside the leaf, water evaporates from moist cell surfaces into the air spaces. When the outside air is drier, water vapor spreads outward overall. Individual molecules move both ways through the opening; it is not a one-way valve. Carbon dioxide also moves both ways, but photosynthesis removes it inside, helping maintain an overall inward flow. Now make the outside air drier while keeping this opening the same size. The greater difference in water vapor makes water loss faster. The leaf can keep gaining carbon, but its water supply may struggle to replace what escapes.

## Beat 3 — Narrow the route

Content needed: Carry the dry-air condition and the same pore into a partial, then near-complete closure driven by coordinated guard-cell shape change. Reduce both net transport streams as the passage narrows. Show a small continuing water-loss route through the leaf covering, without implying a fixed rate or perfect seal. Return to the same leaf with the selected region identified. Reveal the final tradeoff only after both transport consequences are visible.

Narration: In dry conditions, signals in the plant can cause guard cells to lose water and change shape, narrowing the opening. This response does not require the plant to think or choose. A narrower route slows water vapor escaping, helping protect the leaf's water supply. But it also restricts carbon dioxide entering. With less carbon dioxide available, photosynthesis can slow, so the leaf may make less sugar. Closing does not instantly stop every bit of water loss: some can still escape through the covering and any remaining openings. That is the tradeoff: an open route admits carbon more easily and loses water more easily; closing it conserves water while limiting carbon uptake.

draft.markdown:
# A leaf trades water for carbon

## Beat 1 — Carbon needs a way in

Content needed: An idealized leaf and enlarged lower-surface cutaway. Introduce the same guard-cell pair and pore used in all three beats; connected parts remain connected as the gap narrows in beat-3. GOLD dots mean carbon dioxide. Show movement both ways, with net inward movement as leaf cells use carbon dioxide. No water-vapor reveal yet.

Narration: To make sugar using sunlight, a leaf needs carbon dioxide from the air. But much of that work happens inside the leaf. How does the gas get there? Look at this tiny opening in the leaf’s surface. It is called a stoma. The gap leads into air spaces among the leaf’s cells. The gold dots represent carbon dioxide. Molecules move through the opening in both directions. As cells use carbon dioxide for photosynthesis, more can enter than leave. An open pore helps keep that carbon supply coming.

## Beat 2 — The same gap lets water out

Content needed: Keep the same open pore. BLUE dots mean water vapor from moist internal cell surfaces. Establish evaporation, then movement through the pore. Drier outside air supports net outward vapor movement while GOLD carbon dioxide has net inward movement. Paths are illustrative, not measurements or a one-for-one swap.

Narration: Now follow the blue dots: water. The surfaces of cells inside the leaf are moist. Some of that water evaporates into the air spaces as water vapor. The same opening that admits carbon dioxide also gives this vapor a route out. When the outside air is drier, more water vapor moves outward than inward. The opening does not sort the gases or exchange one water molecule for one carbon dioxide molecule. Both move through it. So gaining access to carbon dioxide also exposes the leaf to water loss.

## Beat 3 — A smaller gap has two effects

Content needed: Start with the same open pore and both gases. Guard-cell shape changes narrow the gap; show reduced passage for both species under the same outside conditions. Explain the response without conscious intent. Retain some water loss through other routes; closing a pore must not appear to seal the whole leaf.

Narration: In dry conditions, water loss can become difficult to replace. Signals within the plant change the water content and shape of the guard cells around the pore, narrowing the opening. The plant does not think through a choice; this is a biological response. With a smaller gap, less water vapor escapes through that route. But less carbon dioxide can enter, too, which can limit photosynthesis. Closing helps conserve water; it does not instantly stop all water loss. Some water can still escape through other routes. That is the tradeoff: the opening supports sugar-making while also letting precious water leave.
